Article Title: 'Put boxers first': Former World Boxing chief's message to warring BFI factions
Article Text:
Left to right: Boxing Federation of India's Ajay Singh, Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya and former World Boxing chief Boris van der Vorst. (Photo by special arrangement)

New Delhi:

BFI chief Ajay Singh (L) with former World Boxing head Boris van der Vorst.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former World Boxing president Boris van der Vorst has called on India's boxing administrators to put aside their differences and ensure stability within the Boxing Federation of India (BFI), warning that the sport cannot afford organisational uncertainty with larger focus on Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.With Indian boxing enjoying a successful run on the international stage -- winning 7 medals at the Commonwealth Games and 6 at the Asian Games -- van der Vorst believes the priority should be to protect the progress made rather than allow administrative disagreements to affect the sport's preparations for the next Olympic cycle.In an exclusive interaction with TimesofIndia.com, the former World Boxing chief said India's boxing leadership needed to come together behind the current administration of president Ajay Singh , with the interests of athletes taking precedence over everything else."Everyone needs now to be focused on this Olympic podium mission. That's what everyone needs to come together for, work together and take care that there will be stability and continuity for Indian boxing," van der Vorst told TimesofIndia.com.The crisis has been brewing since October 8, when BFI secretary general Pramod Kumar issued a notice seeking a no-confidence motion against Singh. The motion cited alleged unilateral decision-making, unauthorised constitutional amendments, intimidation of state associations, financial irregularities and administrative overreach.Kumar's faction further claimed that 28 of the federation's 35 affiliated units had backed the move. Singh's camp, however, questioned the legality of the proposed meeting and maintained that the process did not follow the federation's constitution.The dispute escalated, when Singh and Kumar suspended each other. Singh cited alleged financial irregularities, non-cooperation with investigations and misuse of authority in his action against Pramod Kumar. The secretary general subsequently issued a suspension order against the president, pending the outcome of the no-confidence motion. Both sides accused each other of violating the BFI constitution.The proposed October 28 Special General Meeting (SGM) was subsequently put on hold by the Punjab and Haryana High Court until November 13, following a petition filed by Singh.That did not stop the opposition from making its presence felt. On October 28, representatives claiming the support of 28 of BFI's 35 affiliated units and eight of its 13 executive committee members met Union Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) CEO Raghuram Iyer. The faction submitted a memorandum alleging governance lapses and seeking intervention, including the formation of an independent ad-hoc committee and fresh elections.Against this backdrop, van der Vorst believes the focus must shift back to the athletes and the opportunities ahead. He credited Ajay Singh and BFI's Executive Director Col. Arun Malik for the progress made by Indian boxing, pointing to the investment in the high-performance programme and the exposure provided to boxers through international competitions."I think the most important thing is taking good care under the current leadership for the rough talents and diamonds that are already available for many years," he said.Recalling his early visits to India, van der Vorst said he had recognised the potential at grassroots gyms and believed the country could become a boxing powerhouse if the talent was nurtured correctly.He pointed to the depth India now possesses across weight categories, with three or four boxers capable of competing at the highest level in several divisions."You have to thank, of course, the current president Ajay Singh for doing this and also the great team of Col. Arun Malik, who took care of the talents in the high-performance squad," he said.With the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away and the qualification pathway approaching, van der Vorst said Indian boxing needed continuity in its preparations."It is the responsibility now of all the boxing leaders here in India to look into the mirror and say to yourself, how can we contribute to this important mission and support the leadership of Ajay Singh and Col. Arun Malik," he said."By putting the interest of the boxers first, you take care that the current leadership can do their work," he stated.
Article Summary: Boris van der Vorst calls on India's boxing administrators to put aside their differences and ensure stability within the Boxing Federation of India. The former World Boxing chief says the sport cannot afford organisational uncertainty with larger focus on Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. The crisis has been brewing since October 8, when BFI secretary general Pramod Kumar issued a notice seeking a no-confidence motion against Singh.

Article Title: Two Bristol teenage brothers build a £100 Braille printer inspired by their blind grandfather, win international award and plan to make the design free for everyone
Article Text:
How two Bristol brothers built a £100 Braille printer

Their grandfather's experience helped shape the idea

International recognition at the World Robot Olympiad

Why the brothers want to make the design free

Two brothers from Bristol have won international recognition for developing a portable Braille printer that can be built for around £100, offering a more affordable way to produce printed material for blind and partially sighted people. Tom Hunt, 19, and his younger brother Felix, 16, created the device, called BrailleGo!, after becoming aware of the difficulties people and organisations face in accessing Braille documents. Their grandfather, a Yorkshire-born engineer who contributed to the early development of the Jodrell Bank Observatory, lost his sight in his sixties, helping inspire their work. The brothers received the Best Start-Up Idea award at the 2026 World Robot Olympiad European Open Championship in Zagreb, Croatia. They now plan to release the printer’s design files, code and assembly instructions as an open-source project.BrailleGo! is a compact device designed to produce short-run Braille documents, including children's books, museum guides, public information leaflets and meeting agendas. The brothers developed it under the team name Hunt Robotics, using readily available components and 3D-printed parts to keep the cost down.Commercial Braille embossers can cost more than £1,000 and may be bulky, making them difficult to access for individuals and smaller organisations with limited budgets. By contrast, the brothers estimate that BrailleGo! can be built for around £100.The printer is intended to address situations in which only a small number of Braille copies are needed. Rather than relying on expensive equipment for every printing requirement, organisations could potentially use a more affordable device to produce material for specific events, activities or visitors.The brothers' grandfather was an engineer from Yorkshire who contributed to the early development of the Jodrell Bank Observatory. He lost his sight in his sixties, giving the family a personal connection to the challenges faced by people living with sight loss.Their mother’s volunteering with the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB) also helped Tom and Felix understand the difficulties people and organisations can encounter when trying to access printed Braille material.These experiences encouraged them to explore how engineering could help make such resources more accessible. Their aim was not simply to build a working printer, but to develop one that people could reproduce without needing to invest in expensive specialist equipment.The brothers represented the UK at the 2026 World Robot Olympiad European Open Championship, held in Zagreb, Croatia, in October. Their project received the competition's Best Start-Up Idea prize.BrailleGo! also placed second in the Senior Future Innovators category, according to the competition's results. The event brought together 220 national-winning teams from 45 countries under the theme Robots Meet Culture, which challenged participants to explore how technology could improve access to arts, heritage and cultural experiences.The judging panel praised the printer's technical quality, including its 3D design and electronics, as well as the brothers' teamwork and focus on a real-world problem. Judges also noted that the pair had developed the device independently, without support from a coding or maker club.For Tom, who began studying Design Engineering at the University of Bristol in September, the recognition marked an important moment in a project that involved designing and building a machine capable of producing readable Braille.Instead of focusing on commercialising BrailleGo!, Tom and Felix plan to make its code, design files and assembly instructions freely available as an open-source project. This would allow people in different communities to build the printer, adapt it to their needs and potentially improve the design.Making the plans available could help extend the idea beyond the brothers' own project, giving schools, community groups and organisations supporting people with sight loss an opportunity to explore a lower-cost approach to Braille printing.Tom said he hoped others would build on their work once the designs were shared. His younger brother Felix described the competition in Croatia as an opportunity to meet teams from around the world and learn from their projects, adding that building the printer had taught him about engineering, problem-solving and teamwork.Eleanor Southwood, director of impact and external affairs at sight-loss charity Fight for Sight, praised the concept, highlighting the potential uses of an affordable, portable printer for producing smaller quantities of Braille material.
Article Summary: Tom Hunt, 19, and his younger brother Felix, 16, created the device, called BrailleGo! It is designed to produce short-run Braille documents, including children's books, museum guides, public information leaflets and meeting agendas. The brothers received the Best Start-Up Idea award at the 2026 World Robot Olympiad European Open Championship in Zagreb, Croatia. They now plan to release the printer’s design files, code and assembly instructions as an open- source project.

Article Title: Mahjong finds a seat at the Diwali party table
Article Text:
Ria Bajaj and Manek Jain Daswani enjoying a round of Mahjong with their friends

‘Now most Diwali parties have a Mahjong setup or two’

From intimate gatherings to elaborate festive celebrations, the game seems to have found its way into every party calendar. And unlike games where guests can join in for a quick round before moving to the next party, Mahjong seems to have everyone glued to their seats

‘Mahjong is replacing games like Rummy and Teen Patti’

‘People are requesting crash courses for the game’





What once used to be a popular social engagement among Indian army wives in cantonment towns has now made inroads in Delhi’s elite circle as its favourite party game. The popularity of Mahjong, a 19th century Chinese tile game, started making news last year. From then to now it has skyrocketed to an extent that Mahjong has acquired a high table at Diwali parties. The game’s social status and engagement score even seem to exceed the popularity of traditional games like Teen Patti at Diwali parties. Now, a setup or two for Mahjong with highly engrossed players has become a common sight at parties this festive season.Fashion designer Ritu Beri, a proud Army kid who’s grown up watching her mother play Mahjong, shares that she is surprised at how the game, which she saw her mom playing all her life, has now become the talk of the town. “In the Army, it was the one game that everyone played, there was no Rummy or anything else, for army wives it was only Mahjong. I still remember my mom had the most beautiful ivory Mahjong set, a rare set. It is so nostalgic for me when someone says, ‘Let’s meet over Mahjong,’” she tells us.The ‘game of luck and strategy’ has been popular at theme parties, and we have been told that there is “hardly any upscale kitty party that doesn’t have Mahjong.”Given its popularity, it is understandable when we are told that Karwa Chauth Mahjong events and parties were a hit this festive season.“I do Mahjong events and parties with my friends regularly and it was one of the most appropriate fit for a Karwa Chauth gathering. This game keeps you engrossed, you actually can spend hours playing it. Once you start playing, it gets so interesting that you lose track of time. Now most Delhi parties have Mahjong setups and it is as popular as card games, even more,” says Sunayana Bhinder Chibba, who has been organising Mahjong parties for her friends.Along with parties, there are also festive events being organised by Mahjong-exclusive clubs with hundreds of members across cities. The growing interest has also turned Mahjong into a reason to host a party rather than just as an activity. From private sessions among friends to larger gatherings organised by clubs, the game has acquired a social calendar of its own. Mumbai-based Ria Bajaj, co-founder of The Mahjong Network, shares, “Ever since the beginning of the festive season, we have been flooded with queries to arrange Mahjong events and private parties. We have an event or a party happening every two days in the city and requests are still pouring in.”And while Mahjong may have traditionally been associated with women’s social gatherings, its growing popularity is now drawing interest from everyone. So much so that even restaurants are looking to cash in on the trend by adding Mahjong to their festive celebrations. Maneka Jain Daswani, Ria’s partner and co-founder of The Mahjong Network based in Delhi, adds, “This festive season Diwali card parties are being replaced by Mahjong parties as it is no longer a ladies’ game. It will be safe to say that Mahjong is fast replacing party games like Rummy or Teen Patti.”The spike in Mahjong’s popularity has also led to many seeking crash courses for the game, especially in the festive season. Noida-based Mahjong coach from Indian Mahjong Association, Vineeta Sahni, who has been playing Mahjong for over three decades now and is also teaching the game now, says that she has been getting requests every day from people who want to learn Mahjong in a couple of hours. “Some people are only seeing this as a social engagement activity and to be a part of the circle, they are looking for crash courses, but the game is not learnt this way. We conduct sessions to introduce the game, provide tables and even train individuals who are interested in learning the game. We recommend a three-hour class to learn and I think five classes are essential. During the festive season, we are witnessing a demand for trainers by those hosting Mahjong parties,” says Vineeta.
Article Summary: Mahjong, a 19th century Chinese tile game, started making news last year. Now, a setup or two for Mahjong with highly engrossed players has become a common sight at parties this festive season. The spike in Mahjong’s popularity has also led to many seeking crash courses for the game.

Article Title: Diwali and the politics of gifting
Article Text:
The bigger question isn’t what to gift, but how to match last year’s generosity without appearing either stingy or extravagant





It is that time of the year again when a subtle realisation occurs that gifting in NCR is no less than any competitive sport. Each year, you prepare in advance, armed with lessons from the last festive season, only to realise that there are more waiting for you this season. And no matter how well you think you know your friend circle, there are always surprises. Someone sends a luxury hamper, and suddenly your box of mithai or dry fruits looks inadequate. The bigger question isn’t what to gift, but how to match last year’s generosity without appearing either stingy or extravagant. Plus, there could be added pressure if you are known as someone who always sends a gift of a certain value. You go lower than that, friends and relatives might assume (and gossip) that you are broke. You spend more, and there might be questions raised about ‘where is all this money coming from?’ Clearly, there is no winning this game.A month before the festive season begins, a budget is earmarked for Diwali gifting. There are categories within that budget, as per the hierarchy of gifting – one for neighbours, friends and acquaintances, a slightly more personalised, better gift for close friends, and a premium range for business associates.And for some, there is an added category for those who unexpectedly turn up with a gift close to Diwali. Of course, the hierarchy isn’t always determined by how close you are to someone. There are people you meet once a year but cannot afford to leave out of your gifting list, and then there are friends who would be perfectly happy sharing a box of mithai with you. The tricky part is deciding who belongs where, because getting the category wrong could mean an entire year of awkwardness. And just when you think the lists have been finalised, budgets approved and gifts dispatched, someone who wasn’t even on your list sends you an elaborate hamper. Now, what should have been a pleasant surprise becomes a fresh problem. One option is to pick up something from the stack of gifts kept aside specifically for regifting. But the real dilemma arises when the gift you have received looks rather expensive and you have absolutely no intention of spending a similar amount on a return gesture. Do you send something modest and hope they don’t notice the difference? Do you make anexception and stretch your budget? Or do you simply thank them profusely and hope that gratitude counts as reciprocation?Then comes the rather delicate business of regifting. While most people have no qualms about passing on an unopened box of dry fruits or an elaborate festive hamper, one has to be extremely careful about where it came from and where it is headed. The last thing you want is for a gift to find its way back to the person who originally sent it.There is also the question of whether a gift needs to be personally delivered or whether sending it through a driver is enough. Does dropping it off at the gate count as a festive gesture? Should you call to check if it has been received? And if someone makes the effort to personally deliver a gift, are you now expected to return the favour with a visit? Suddenly, the gifting exercise begins to resemble the scheduling of Diwali parties, with lists, locations and social obligations to manage. Perhaps the most amusing part of this entire exercise is that while everyone insists that ‘it’s the thought that counts’, an extraordinary amount of thought goes into calculating the value of the gift, the relationship with the recipient and the possible consequences of getting either wrong. By the time Diwali arrives, you have spent so much time deciding on gifting that you begin to wonder whether festive gifting was ever meant to be this complicated.
Article Summary: The bigger question isn’t what to gift, but how to match last year’s generosity without appearing either stingy or extravagant. A month before the festive season, a budget is earmarked for Diwali gifting. The tricky part is deciding who belongs where, because getting the category wrong could mean an entire year of awkwardness.

Article Title: 'Harsh on Jasprit Bumrah to say he’s picking and choosing matches': Shane Bond
Article Text:
Shane Bond, Jasprit Bumrah

Excerpts:

How challenging is it to navigate tight schedules, player availability and preparation?

Both teams have split squads for the ODI series. Is that the right approach when turnaround times are short?

Does match time still trump net practice as preparation?

Does it make sense for Jasprit Bumrah to skip the ODIs ahead of the Test series?

Does workload management become even more important with the ODI World Cup next year?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Is that realistic given the packed Future Tours Programme?

What is your assessment of India’s current pace attack?

With a packed international calendar forcing teams to constantly juggle workloads and preparation, both India and New Zealand have taken steps to keep their key bowlers fresh for the upcoming Test series that will conclude a tour stretching beyond 40 days. Several frontline players were released from the final two ODIs to focus on red-ball cricket, while India opted not to include Jasprit Bumrah in the ODI squad, allowing him to concentrate exclusively on the Tests.In an interview with TOI, former New Zealand pace great Shane Bond discussed the challenges of player management, the value of ODI cricket as Test preparation, and the recurring debate surrounding Bumrah’s availability.It’s a challenge. When I look back at my playing days, the best players in a country would generally play two formats, sometimes all three. The schedule was never as congested as it is now. If you were in the New Zealand team, you were among the best 11, 12 or 13 cricketers in the country. Today, you often see two Indian teams playing simultaneously. New Zealand, too, can field very different squads around the world depending on the schedule.It’s simply part of modern cricket. Personally, I always enjoyed playing One-day cricket before a Test series because, as a bowler, you spent three-and-a-half hours on your feet and delivered 10 overs at high intensity.I felt it was ideal preparation because a two-hour Test session suddenly seemed relatively short. The only challenge was handling those extra overs.Absolutely. Nothing replicates time spent on your feet in a match. You can do all the training and net sessions you want, but it doesn’t compare to standing in the field, running from fine leg to mid-on and maintaining that intensity for six hours.That’s the kind of preparation players need, not just bowling in the nets.There’s often a perception that players are simply picking and choosing what they want to play. I don’t think that’s the case at all. Experienced bowlers understand their bodies very well. They’re constantly discussing their workloads with medical staff and coaches, assessing what they can physically handle.The biggest risk period is always when a player is returning from injury and readjusting to competitive cricket. That’s why I think it’s pretty harsh on Booms (Bumrah) to suggest he’s picking and choosing.It applies not just to Booms but to every player. India play an enormous amount of cricket, so managing workloads is essential. You want your best players fit, fresh and ready when the World Cup arrives next Oct or Nov. Every major cricket nation is trying to achieve the same balance, especially with the demands of both international and franchise cricket.It’s extremely difficult. Australia, for example, are currently in South Africa before heading home, and then they have a four-Test series against New Zealand. They’re working hard to protect their fast bowlers. New Zealand, too, want their best pace attack available for that Australia tour.It’s a constant challenge for coaches, trainers and support staff around the world.I’m a huge fan of Mohammed Siraj. I love his energy and body language. He’s been performing consistently across formats for a long time. India have a very well-balanced attack. The one thing they perhaps lack is a left-arm fast bowler, but they’ve got height, pace and skill. They hit the seam hard and, importantly, they have depth.Even someone like Aquib Nabi has come through and looks a quality bowler. Akash Deep is a good bowler too. As a coach, Gautam Gambhir will want enough options to rest and rotate players, and India certainly have that luxury.
Article Summary: India and New Zealand have split squads for the ODI series. Several frontline players were released from the final two ODIs to focus on red-ball cricket, while India opted not to include Jasprit Bumrah in the squad, allowing him to concentrate exclusively on the Tests.

Article Title: ‘2018 closure of Mohammed Ali Road Urdu school signalled big educational, cultural loss’
Article Text:
Shut Urdu school at Mohammed Ali Road, Mumbai

Mumbai:





In one of his celebrated ghazals, legendary poet Mirza Ghalib (1797–1869) likens this world to bazeecha-e-atfal or a children’s playground where a tamasha or spectacle is enacted every day.Replace Ghalib with Ismail Beg Muhammad High School at Mohammed Ali Road, and it might, like the poet, strike a note, complaining about the games the world is playing with it. Except that the five-storey school building, amid chaotic traffic and a busy bazaar, stands quiet, and children have not played any pranks or games since 2018 when it shut.Located opposite the iconic Minara Masjid across the road, life goes as usual around the school. Shops selling footwear, perfume, designer hijab and a hakim’s clinic out of the school building’s commercial spaces do brisk business. A notice of a bank that operated from the ground floor until recently informs customers about the new address nearby.The school’s closure, complains local resident Shoaib Khatib in a viral video clip, is a big educational and cultural loss.“Generations of students studied here and many of them are well-placed in India and abroad.The school’s closure symbolises a collective loss to the locals,” says Khatib, an alumnus of the school and ex-trustee of the iconic Juma Masjid of Bombay.Perhaps few know this school, founded in 1936, better than Sohail Lokhandwala, ex-principal (1988-2000). “With over 700 students and 30 staff, this school reverberated with life. It nurtured many first-generation learners. It took under its wings students mostly from underprivileged families or those who wanted quality education in Urdu,” recalls Lokhandwala, also a former MLA. Lokhandwala says the school fell on bad days once the old, committed trustees, including its chairman Salim Ismail Beg Muhammad, died in 2016.Businessman-educationist Nasir Jamal grew up in the area. “I cannot forget the day I took my friend and cousin (maternal uncle’s son) Shahabuddin bhai for admission in fourth or fifth class. Later my siblings too studied here. There was no need to shut the school. They could have switched from Urdu to English medium,” says Jamal.Congress MLA Amin Patel, whose office is a few minutes’ walk from the school, says he has spoken to the trustees and suggested a change in medium from Urdu to English by keeping Urdu as a subject. “This is not the first vernacular school in the city which has faced paucity of pupils. I have spoken to the trustees and told them that they must restart it with a changed medium by keeping Urdu as a subject,” says Patel.We meet Abu Bakar Salim, son of the last chief trustee Salim Ismail Beg Muhammad. He says he has been a trustee since 1988 but did not take much interest in the school affairs till his father was alive.It was Salim’s grandfather Abu Bakar Abdurahman Beg Muhammad, a philanthropist, who built this school, naming it after his uncle Ismail Beg Muhammad despite strong opposition from many conservative Muslims who wanted a mosque here.The founder, says Lokhandwala, was a progressive Muslim who even petitioned Bombay High Court, arguing that the area already had many mosques and a school was needed here. The British judge favoured the school plan.As one leaves looking at the school’s locked gates, the muezzins at Minara, Hamidiya and many other mosques call out azan for the evening prayers. The founder’s original dream stays halted as uncertainty looms over the school’s fate.
Article Summary: Ismail Beg Muhammad High School at Mohammed Ali Road, Mumbai, shut in 2018. The five-storey school building, amid chaotic traffic and a busy bazaar, stands quiet. The founder, says Sohail Lokhandwala, was a progressive Muslim who even petitioned Bombay High Court.

Article Title: First on-camera tiger sighting by tourists recorded at Radhanagari-Dajipur sanctuary
Article Text:
Male Tiger STR-T10 at Dajipur Wildlife Sanctuary

Kolhapur





: Tourists visiting Radhanagari-Dajipur Wildlife Sanctuary had a rare wildlife encounter on Monday morning when they caught a glimpse of a male Bengal tiger.The big cat, identified as STR-T10 ‘Ranoji’, was spotted during a jungle safari in the sanctuary’s core zone. Forest department officials said this is the first time a tiger has been officially sighted and recorded on camera by tourists in Dajipur sanctuary, with both photographs and video footage verifying the event.The thrilling encounter took place just a day after the forest department officially resumed wildlife safaris for the new tourism season on Nov 1.Safari vehicle driver Prasad Korgaonkar, who was guiding three tourists from Rukadi, described the moment. “This was my very first ride since safaris resumed. During the trek, we first came across a jungle hen, a snake, and a gaur, before suddenly spotting Ranoji resting under a canopy of trees. While we regularly see gaurs in this region, witnessing a wild tiger was an unforgettable, thrilling experience.”Wildlife experts said the landmark sighting reinforces the ecological importance of the 341 sq km sanctuary, which serves as a vital corridor within the larger Sahyadri Tiger Reserve.Forest authorities attributed the successful sighting to strict conservation measures aimed at reducing human disturbance. The wildlife department has capped the number of active safari vehicles and restricted tour timings to a specific window between 6am and 2pm. Additionally, forest officials have dug 20 artificial water bodies throughout the sanctuary to ensure adequate drinking supply for the wildlife. To maintain strict safety standards and operational order, every safari vehicle is mandated to carry a registered guide.
Article Summary: Tourists visiting Radhanagari-Dajipur Wildlife Sanctuary had a rare wildlife encounter on Monday morning when they caught a glimpse of a male Bengal tiger. The big cat, identified as STR-T10 ‘Ranoji’, was spotted during a jungle safari in the sanctuary’s core zone. Forest department officials said this is the first time a tiger has been officially sighted and recorded on camera.

Article Title: Mumbai-bound traffic hit after hatchback catches fire on Vashi Creek bridge
Article Text:
The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine.





NAVI MUMBAI: Vehicular traffic from Navi Mumbai towards Mumbai was disrupted for around 30 minutes after a hatchback caught fire while crossing the Vashi Creek Bridge on Friday at around 7.30pm.The driver escaped unhurt. He immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. However, the fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred.Vashi traffic police alerted the Vashi fire brigade, which reached the spot within 15 minutes. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.Sunil Kadam, senior inspector of the Vashi traffic unit, said the driver was identified as Sumit Bhikaji Kadam.“At around 7.45pm, we received a call from one Rahul, whose full name is not known, informing us that a car had caught fire on the Mumbai-bound lane of the Vashi Creek Bridge,” said AV Sisode, the on-duty fireman at Vashi fire station.“In the meantime, we also received a call from the Vashi traffic police and immediately rushed to the spot with a fire tender.
